COURIER HITS

By: Nicky Troll | Delivery

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Gun-wielding robbers target easy-to-hit courier vans transporting high-value goods in organised hits that feed a global black market for mobile devices.

Unique Selling Point:
CRIME TREND // VIDEO FOOTAGE // INDUSTRY INSIDER SPILLING THE BEANS ON INEFFECTIVE INDUSTRY STRATEGIES TO DEAL WITH CRIME TREND // HUMAN INTEREST - DRIVERS AT RISK

Summary:
Courier Hits are a growing crime trend with both sophisticated syndicates and opportunistic thugs targeting companies transporting high value goods.

We investigated this sudden spike, the affect it has on the drivers who are faced with gun-wielding robbers and explore the impact it has on the economy in terms of security costs and the global black market for stolen mobile devices.


Further information:
The reality is that no one thinks of the courier industry as a security operation but in the current economic climate with constant criminal threats, businesses have had to adapt in order to protect their cargos.

This is an issue affecting the entire courier industry – bigger role players are targeted in organised hits, while smaller companies are hit by opportunistic criminals taking a chance in the hopes of scoring with value cargo. Couriers are being targeted because they are highly visible within the public space, making them soft targets for thieves.

INDUSTRY VOICE - Gary Marshall, SA Express Parcel Association.
Marshall will give context to the challenges from a business perspective and to highlight some of the innovative approaches that they have to incorporate in the daily running of their business.

While there are no accurate figures available regarding robberies of couriers, Marshall explains anecdotal evidence from these companies suggested that the problem was on the rise. “When I speak to our members, they reckon it is worse now than it has ever been.”

UNDERREPORTING
Marshall explains: “A lot of these are reported as armed robberies, and some of them are reported as hijackings, and I think many of them are not reported at all. Part of the problem is that once you report it, the vehicle becomes a crime scene, and it may get impounded, therefore the courier can’t continue delivering.”

VIOLENCE
These robbers come with hand guns and R5’s they block off traffic and are not afraid to pull the trigger. In one the most recent incidents in March, a security guard was shot and killed.

**|THERE ARE A NUMBER OF VIDEO CLIPS SHOWING ARMED ROBBERS TAKING ON COURIER COMPANIES. I’M BUSY TRYING TO SOURCE WAREHOUSE ROBBERY FOOTAGE TOO.

We will be interviewing a driver that has been hit a few times to bring in the human element of fear and the level of danger experienced on a daily basis.

THE ECONOMICS OF COURIER HITS
Courier companies were incurring major costs on all kinds of security mechanisms and controls to protect their facilities, assets, and employees. Expenses often include costs of escort vehicles, camera systems, vehicle tracking systems, control centres, helicopters, and follow-up vehicles. Unfortunately these costs tend to get built into courier prices, so the public will pay for it at the end of the day.

We will interview a security company doing armed escorts that will explain some of the challenges, how they’ve adapted strategy to deal with these attacks and the spike in violence. This company has dash cam and internal camera footage of the guard cars.

BIGGER PICTURE
Where do cellphones go and the fact that the stolen devices re–enter the market either with new IMEI numbers or alternately get exported.

INSIDE SCOOP : HIDDEN ID RISK INVESTIGATOR FOR COURIER COMPANY
This is someone that will give an understanding of the modus operandi, to paint a picture of the global syndicated crime network behind the black market for stolen cellphones and to explain the challenges of these types of investigations. The biggest challenge at this stage is that courier companies are tackling this crime threat in silos – they are not working together and are not sharing security intelligence.

The robbers that have been identified have also been linked to CIT robberies – some have even been charged previously – showing the level of criminal expertise being used in these hits and the fact that criminals will evolve and adapt their MOs to perpetrate crime.

GLOBAL CELLPHONE TRACKING EXPERT
I have tried to get someone locally, but that seems to be a dead end. I have now reached out to three international organisations and I am hopeful that one of them will come through for a Zoom interview.

This will be someone that can explain that these phones show up all over the world and that there are challenges with how phones are currently exported out of countries, how crime trends internationally compare to SA in that globally criminal activity across warehousing, road freight and retail stores within the operator’s supply chain also result in large volumes of counterfeit or grey devices hitting the market.

STRUCTURE

VO: Living in Lockdown has popularised online shopping around the globe with an estimated 1.8 billion active ecommerce shoppers - packages are delivered day in and day out across South Africa.

LINK: But with convenience there comes a new threat. Gun-wielding criminals target courier companies as they transport high value goods in dramatic hits carried out with military precision.

VO: With multiple hits across the country every day, the R20 billion local courier industry is under siege.

GARRY: It's like a war zone for them out there.

VO: Garry Marshall, is from SAEPA, the South African Express Parcel Association, representing the courier industry. He says, some of his members experience up to 3 hits a day.

GARRY: We're everywhere and we're highly visible. // We have thousands of vehicles on the road in Johannesburg alone. // we don't carry toothpaste as a rule. So people understand that there's this commodity of value in there.

VO: Millions of rands worth of cargo is transported in and around major cities daily from electronics to mobile devices. Criminal syndicates have set their sights on these loads, that are quick to move on the black market.

INSIDER: They'll it's getting more aggressive // These guys are heavily armed. They've got rifles, high performance vehicles. They're well equipped to do the job.

VO: This man is an investigator who works within a courier operation. He says normal day to day courier vans are sitting ducks.

INSIDER: // it's soft skin vehicles. It's the easy target. // If God shoots at you in a vehicle like that, what are you going to do? Nothing is going to get shot and that’s that.

LINK: When these robbers go in guns blazing, the courier drivers are usually the ones who are threated first – these criminal gangs are on a mission, desperate to get to the loot, they are ruthless and violent.

DONALD: when they took out guns, I was fearing for my life that maybe they're going to kill us.

VO: Donald Phiri has been a driver for over 20 years. He was held up in July 2020 when he was transporting a shipment of mobile phones. This is exclusive footage from the truck on the day of the robbery.

DONALD: // we stopped by the robots. After two minutes, all of a sudden I saw guys carry guns, almost about 15 guys, 15.

VO: Watch as the gang stands around while, a generator powered industrial grinder is brought out and used to cut the locks on the back of truck.

Once open, they off loaded as many boxes as they can in just over three minutes before making their getaway.

Risk Manager Martin Taylor works for a company specialising in international freight forwarding and warehousing of predominantly high value goods. While some of the stock was recovered in the July robbery, Taylor says it was clearly an orchestrated hit.

MARTIN: in this industry, we’re fighting syndicates at the end of the day, and they are fighting us as much as we sit and plan, they sit and plan

VO: Criminals move between different crime spheres from hijacking to Cash-in Transit robberies and more recently to courier hits. These, are professionals according to Taylor.

MARTIN: The groups are up to twenty five for a single courier vehicle, you know, so how do you fight that, you know, armed gang of twenty five to take out a single courier vehicle driver and maybe one or two escort vehicles, you know, so the groups are just getting stronger. And I would say it's not opportunistic. You know, in the residential areas, you'll have your opportunistic guys that grab a vehicle quickly in front of reside ntial gates. But most of this is syndicate driven.

LINK: No one thinks of the courier industry as a security operation but in the current economic climate with constant criminal threats, businesses have had to adapt in order to protect their cargos.

VO: Robbie Roberts is the head of security for a law enforcement company providing armed escorts in armoured vehicles to the courier industry.

ROBBIE: These Guys doesn't play. They come with high caliber firearms like AK 47 for sure, and also a two to three rifles they also come with high powered vehicles if they need to escape

VO: This is footage from a recent attack on a delivery truck escorted by Roberts’ team.

Watch at the robbers ram the vehicle on the side and open fire. 42 shots pelted the driver’s side of the escort vehicle.

ROBBIE: they've got no sense for life because they go for the kill. // You can see it is not guys that you get from the street//, you can see the way they approach the cargo. // the way that they attack the escorts. You can see these guys take cover they don’t just run around

VO: Here in a second clip captured from the camera on the back of the courier van - you can see how brazen armed robbers relentlessly open fire on the escort vehicle accompanying the courier van. The gunmen continue shooting despite being surrounded by civilian cars at a busy intersection during this robbery in broad daylight.

A few days later, another courier company was hit at the entrance gate of MT’s Head Office in Johannesburg.

Watch a white double cab and silver BMW race to the boom gate. The robbers emerge and open fire.

The thieves shot at the escort car, wounding three of the guards, while the rest of the gang loaded boxes of handsets into the double-cab.

For drivers like Phiri, attacks like this are a daily reality.

DONALD: //It's dangerous because they don't know when it's going to happen. I see this thing now is getting worse every day.

MARTIN: we do the hijacking awareness training and as much as training and trauma counseling that you can do, you know, it's still hits home. You know, it's not just about the driver. It's about the crew that goes with him. At the end of the day, you know, that they safely return home.
¬¬
VO: Courier companies are incurring major costs incorporating a range of security mechanisms and controls to protect their facilities, cargo, and employees. While Taylor’s company has invested heavily in keeping their cargo secure, it doesn’t come cheap.

MARTIN: security, cost is always a cost that you can't recover,// it's not just the initial capital layout, but it's also the monthly cost. //You know, it ultimately affects the logistics cost and then the consumer cost.

VO: Some companies are spending as much as R5 million a month on security explains Marshall.

GARRY: they're suffering enormous financial losses because all of them are carrying these goods and take responsibility for it. So their losses run into a lot of money M8

VO: Big money that the criminals are pocketing. Investigations have revealed that many of the devices are destined for export.

INSIDER: // they can sell it for half the price. And it's clean cash. //They just do what they need to do, get rid of it, take it out of the country and sell it and make money.
MARTIN: you'll find that these devices end up cross-border the very same // I mean, Botswana border post, Mozambican border post that goes over the border within four hours. It's already cross-border undocumented, obviously.

VO: Globally, the massive demand for smartphones has given rise to a booming black market for stolen mobile devices. International syndicates trade sought after electronics under the radar.

Wale Goodluck is from GSMA – an international mobile interest group that operates a global IMEI blacklisting service.

AKINWALE: Cell phone traffic is organized, big time movement of devices across borders, so you find that phones are being stolen in one country and they one unable to activate those phones in that market. Very often the criminal gangs are taking them across borders and going to markets where you may have perhaps less stringent on boarding operational requirements for new phones on the networks.

VO: Internationally, mobile device crime trends have moved from opportunistic petty thieving to organised syndicates carrying out robberies.

AKINWALE: Across the world, I think there's a general trend that mobile phone theft is moving from the sort of personal smash and grab kind of crime and moving more to the more sophisticated phone trafficking Bodleian of warehouses and hijacking transits of large consignments of mobile phones. // that is a global trend and is driven by just the sheer attractiveness of mobile handsets and mobile devices.

VO: The biggest challenge in South Africa is that courier companies are tackling this crime threat in silos and are not sharing security intelligence according this investigator.

MASA: Could the courier companies themselves be to blame for this?
INSIDE R: // they are scared of actually sharing information. And and the guys, everything is close to your body. You don't share with another company. So, you know, it's a problem because if I get it and you get it and you don't tell me about it and the same, I need somebody else. We knew about it

VO: But Marshall is confident that there is a shift taking place, and talks of joint efforts within the industry and police to combat this crime scourge.

GARRY: // We're doing everything possible we can. The amount of money that we're spending, t, the amount of sleepless nights that go into this. // we need more intelligence, we need more cooperation, and that's the only way we're going to tackle it. But it is a South African problem,.

VO: But as long as there is a global demand for cheap mobile devices, criminals will keep coming for the stock and security will have to be stepped up.

MARTIN: It's not one holistic solution at all that can fight this.// looking at criminal trends and as they evolve, we have to evolve. I

MASA: What if we don’t get a handle on this?
ROBBIE: the way these guys are shooting. They don't care. They've got notion for life or people around them. // M19 We're going to end up in a proper bloodbath



PROMOS

PROMO 1: Gun-wielding robbers target high-value goods couriered across the country with military precision. We investigate this growing crime trend feeding the global black market for mobile devices.

PROMO 2: Courier Hits are a growing crime trend with both sophisticated syndicates and opportunistic thugs, targeting companies transporting high value goods. The criminals are brazen and ruthless.

PROMO 3: Despite spending millions of rands to protect high value cargo – the delivery industry is under attack by brazen organised gangs targeting them every day in increasingly violent hits.

metadata.Summary: Courier Hits are a growing crime trend with both sophisticated syndicates and opportunistic thugs targeting companies transporting high value goods. We investigated this sudden spike, the affect it has on the drivers who are faced with gun-wielding robbers and explore the impact it has on the economy in terms of security costs and the global black market for stolen mobile devices.
metadata.Further information: The reality is that no one thinks of the courier industry as a security operation but in the current economic climate with constant criminal threats, businesses have had to adapt in order to protect their cargos. This is an issue affecting the entire courier industry – bigger role players are targeted in organised hits, while smaller companies are hit by opportunistic criminals taking a chance in the hopes of scoring with value cargo. Couriers are being targeted because they are highly visible within the public space, making them soft targets for thieves. INDUSTRY VOICE - Gary Marshall, SA Express Parcel Association. Marshall will give context to the challenges from a business perspective and to highlight some of the innovative approaches that they have to incorporate in the daily running of their business. While there are no accurate figures available regarding robberies of couriers, Marshall explains anecdotal evidence from these companies suggested that the problem was on the rise. “When I speak to our members, they reckon it is worse now than it has ever been.” UNDERREPORTING Marshall explains: “A lot of these are reported as armed robberies, and some of them are reported as hijackings, and I think many of them are not reported at all. Part of the problem is that once you report it, the vehicle becomes a crime scene, and it may get impounded, therefore the courier can’t continue delivering.” VIOLENCE These robbers come with hand guns and R5’s they block off traffic and are not afraid to pull the trigger. In one the most recent incidents in March, a security guard was shot and killed. **|THERE ARE A NUMBER OF VIDEO CLIPS SHOWING ARMED ROBBERS TAKING ON COURIER COMPANIES. I’M BUSY TRYING TO SOURCE WAREHOUSE ROBBERY FOOTAGE TOO. We will be interviewing a driver that has been hit a few times to bring in the human element of fear and the level of danger experienced on a daily basis. THE ECONOMICS OF COURIER HITS Courier companies were incurring major costs on all kinds of security mechanisms and controls to protect their facilities, assets, and employees. Expenses often include costs of escort vehicles, camera systems, vehicle tracking systems, control centres, helicopters, and follow-up vehicles. Unfortunately these costs tend to get built into courier prices, so the public will pay for it at the end of the day. We will interview a security company doing armed escorts that will explain some of the challenges, how they’ve adapted strategy to deal with these attacks and the spike in violence. This company has dash cam and internal camera footage of the guard cars. BIGGER PICTURE Where do cellphones go and the fact that the stolen devices re–enter the market either with new IMEI numbers or alternately get exported. INSIDE SCOOP : HIDDEN ID RISK INVESTIGATOR FOR COURIER COMPANY This is someone that will give an understanding of the modus operandi, to paint a picture of the global syndicated crime network behind the black market for stolen cellphones and to explain the challenges of these types of investigations. The biggest challenge at this stage is that courier companies are tackling this crime threat in silos – they are not working together and are not sharing security intelligence. The robbers that have been identified have also been linked to CIT robberies – some have even been charged previously – showing the level of criminal expertise being used in these hits and the fact that criminals will evolve and adapt their MOs to perpetrate crime. GLOBAL CELLPHONE TRACKING EXPERT I have tried to get someone locally, but that seems to be a dead end. I have now reached out to three international organisations and I am hopeful that one of them will come through for a Zoom interview. This will be someone that can explain that these phones show up all over the world and that there are challenges with how phones are currently exported out of countries, how crime trends internationally compare to SA in that globally criminal activity across warehousing, road freight and retail stores within the operator’s supply chain also result in large volumes of counterfeit or grey devices hitting the market.
